12 CFR Part 745
RIN 3133-AG24
AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) solicits public comment on a proposal to streamline the methods a federally insured credit union (FICU) may use to provide its members with notice of share insurance coverage. The current regulation is overly prescriptive, mandating that a FICU make available hard copies of certain prescribed materials. While a FICU would still be required to provide notice to members, the proposed rule would defer to the FICU on the method used for such notification. Among other methods, a FICU may elect to provide members with a link to updated online resources that will be maintained on the NCUA website. The Board believes the proposed rule will provide greater flexibility, reduce compliance costs for both NCUA and FICUs, and ensure that members are provided with up-to-date information regarding share insurance coverage.
DATES:
Comments must be received by December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments may be submitted in one of the following ways.
(Please send comments by one method only):
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
The docket number for this proposed rule is NCUA-2026-1888. Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions. If you are reading this document on
federalregister.gov,
you may use the green “SUBMIT A PUBLIC COMMENT” button beneath this rulemaking's title to submit a comment to the
regulations.gov
docket. A plain language summary of the proposed rule is also available on the docket website.

Address to Melane Conyers-Ausbrooks, Secretary of the Board, National Credit Union Administration, 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, Virginia 22314-3428.

Same as mailing address.

Do not include any personally identifiable information (such as name, address, or other contact information) or confidential business information that you do not want publicly disclosed. If you are unable to access public comments on the internet, you may contact the NCUA for alternative access by calling (703) 518-6540 or emailing

.

Ariel Pereira or Thomas Zells, Senior Attorneys, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540, or by mail at National Credit Union Administration, at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
A. Background
NCUA insures funds maintained in accounts of members or those otherwise eligible to maintain insured accounts (member accounts) at FICUs, protects the members who own FICUs, and charters and regulates federal credit unions (FCUs).
[
1
]
NCUA administers the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (Share Insurance Fund). Backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, the Share Insurance Fund provides Federal share insurance to millions of account holders in FICUs.
Under the FCU Act, NCUA is responsible for paying share insurance to any member, or to any person with funds lawfully held in a member account, in the event of a FICU's failure, up to the standard maximum share insurance amount, which is currently set at $250,000.
[
2
]
The FCU Act states the determination of the net amount of share insurance paid “shall be in accordance with such regulations as the Board may prescribe.”
[
3
]
The Board's share insurance regulations are codified in
12 CFR part 745
. Section 745.13 currently requires each FICU to “provide notice to its members concerning NCUA insurance coverage of member accounts” and lists several ways a FICU may comply with this requirement. This section also requires FICUs to make copies of the relevant materials available to their members on request.
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this proposed rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. As noted, the FCU Act grants NCUA specific authority to draft share insurance regulations.
[
4
]
Further, under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for FICUs.
[
5
]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
6
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
7
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
8
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the credit union industry and the Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
II. Proposed Rule
The Board's share insurance regulation at § 745.13 requires that each FICU “provide notice to its members concerning NCUA insurance coverage of member accounts.” Moreover, the regulation specifies the methods a FICU may use to comply with the notification requirement. Specifically, § 745.13 provides that a FICU may comply with the notification requirement by placing “either a copy of part 745 of these rules, the appendix [to part 745], or one or more copies of the NCUA brochure `Your Insured Funds' in each branch office and main office of the credit
(
printed page 66538)
union.”
[
9
]
Copies of these materials must also be made available to members upon request. Thus, while the regulation lists options and does not make them exclusive, it ultimately does require FICUs to provide physical copies of materials, which necessarily leads to costs for those FICUs.
Upon reconsideration, the Board has determined that the regulation imposes an unnecessary cost on both NCUA and FICUs. For NCUA, § 745.13 requires that the agency assume the administrative and staff costs associated with periodically reviewing and updating the “Your Insurance Funds” brochure, which is currently 64 pages long, and arranging and paying for the production and distribution of some brochures. FICUs must incur the costs of purchasing or printing and making the hard copy materials readily available to members. The regulation is also unnecessarily prescriptive in requiring such hard copies, given the ready availability of the part 745 regulations online at the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) website.
[
10
]
Further, the eCFR is updated on a daily basis, thereby ensuring it always contains the most up-to-date version of the regulations.
[
11
]
To the contrary, a FICU must dispose of existing hard copies and print a new version of 12 CFR part 745 each time the regulation is amended. In addition, the NCUA's website contains up-to-date information about share insurance coverage.
For the above reasons, the Board has decided to issue this proposed rule, which would amend § 745.13 to simply provide that each FICU “shall provide notice to its members concerning NCUA insurance coverage of member accounts.”
[
12
]
As part of this rulemaking, NCUA intends to discontinue the “Your Insurance Funds” brochure and will undertake an update of its share insurance coverage website to ensure its comprehensiveness, clarity, and ease of navigation.
[
13
]
The updated website will provide FICUs and their members with a dynamic and up-to-date resource for information regarding share insurance requirements. At the same time, this resource will be freely available to FICUs and their members.
As is true under the existing regulation, revised § 745.13 would not prescribe the timing for providing the required notice. However, NCUA's expectation is that notice will be provided at a logical point in time that is beneficial to members, which would include upon request by a member. For example, a FICU could, if it chose, provide the notice at account opening or other logical time. In addition, revised § 745.13 would defer to the FICU on the method used for providing the required notification. NCUA's expectation is that a FICU will elect a reasonable method that provides members with authoritative information about share insurance coverage. For example, a FICU could, if it chose, continue to make hard copies available or elect to provide members with a link to NCUA's website or the eCFR. In updating its share insurance coverage website, NCUA will consider ease of printing to facilitate the provision of hard copies for those FICUs that elect to do so.
The Board believes the proposed rule would provide greater flexibility, reduce compliance costs for both NCUA and FICUs, ensure that members and others are provided with up-to-date information regarding share insurance coverage, and allow FICUs to provide the information through digital means. The Board welcomes public comment on all aspects of the proposal.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023
The Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 (
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
) (Act) requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include the internet address of a summary of not more than 100 words in length of a proposed rule, in plain language, that shall be posted on the internet website under section 206(d) of the E-Government Act of 2002 (
44 U.S.C. 3501 note
) (commonly known as
regulations.gov
). The Act, under its terms, applies to notices of proposed rulemaking and does not expressly include other types of documents that the Board publishes voluntarily for public comment, such as notices and interim-final rules that request comment despite invoking “good cause” to forgo such notice and public procedure. The Board, however, has elected to address the Act's requirement in these types of documents in the interests of administrative consistency and transparency.
In summary, the Board solicits public comment on a proposal to streamline the methods a FICU may use to provide its members with notice of share insurance coverage. The current regulation is overly prescriptive, mandating that a FICU make available hard copies of certain prescribed materials. While a FICU would still be required to provide notice to members, the proposed rule would defer to the FICU on the method used for such notification.
The proposal and the required summary can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
14
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
15
]
This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this proposed rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
16
]
This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This proposed rule is expected to be an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
(
printed page 66539)
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
17
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
18
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
19
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
The proposed rule would streamline the method a FICU may use to provide its members with notice of share insurance coverage. Under the proposal, a FICU would no longer be required to make available hard copies of certain prescribed materials. FICUs would instead have the flexibility to satisfy the notice requirements by providing members with a link to online resources. Accordingly, to the extent that the proposed rule has any economic impacts on small FICUs, it would be to reduce the costs borne by such credit unions. Neither the current economic burden imposed by the current regulation nor the concomitant reduction resulting from the proposed rule is likely significant, being limited to the staff-time and costs of printing the materials. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and notwithstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. The PRA applies to rulemaking in which an agency creates new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. NCUA has reviewed this proposed rule and determined that it does not create any new or revise any existing collections of information. Accordingly, no PRA submissions to OMB will be made with respect to this rule.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages independent regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
20
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. This proposed rule would only impact NCUA's regulations related to federal share insurance coverage; it would not alter NCUA's relationship or division of responsibilities with state regulatory agencies or bodies. This proposal would not have a substantial direct effect on the states, on the connection between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. NCUA has determined that this proposal does not constitute a policy that has federalism implications for the purposes of the executive order.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
NCUA has determined that this proposed rule would not affect family well-being within the meaning of Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
21
]
The regulatory requirements that are the subject of this proposed rule are exclusively concerned with notice requirements. To the extent the proposal has any impact on families, it would be beneficial by helping families make better informed financial decisions that implicate NCUA share insurance. However, the potential positive effect on family well-being, including financial well-being is, at most, indirect because the proposed rule would not materially change the information provided to the public about share insurance coverage.

AGENCY:
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
ACTION:
Notice of a modified system of records.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB or Bureau) proposes to modify a current Privacy Act System of Records Notice (SORN) titled, “CFPB.001—Freedom of Information Act/Privacy Act System.” This modification clarifies the purpose of the SORN, the categories of records and individuals, the legal authorities, the system manager, the system location address, and the records retention schedule, and introduces a new routine use to permit the disclosure of records to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) or other Federal agencies for records inspection purposes.
DATES:
Comments must be received no later than November 20, 2026. The new system of records will be effective November 20, 2026 unless the comments received result in a contrary determination.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by the title and docket number (
see
above), by any of the following methods:
Electronic:
http://www.regulations.gov
:
Follow the instructions for soliciting comments. A brief summary of this document will be available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​CFPB-2026-0023
.
Email:
privacy@cfpb.gov
.
Include Docket No. CFPB-2026-0023 in the subject line of the email.
Mail/Hand Delivery/Courier:
Kathryn Fong, Chief Privacy Officer, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024; (202) 435-7058. Because paper mail in the Washington, DC area and at
(
printed page 66552)
CFPB is subject to delay, commenters are encouraged to submit comments electronically.
All submissions must include the agency name and docket number for this notice. In general, all comments received will be posted without change to
http://www.regulations.gov
.
All comments, including attachments and other supporting materials, will become part of the public record and subject to public disclosure. You should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. Sensitive personal information, such as account numbers or Social Security numbers, should not be included.

Kathryn Fong, Chief Privacy Officer, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024; (202) 435-7058. If you require this document in an alternative electronic format, please contact

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974 (Privacy Act),
5 U.S.C. 552a
, the CFPB is modifying a system of records titled, “CFPB.001—Freedom of Information Act/Privacy Act System.” The modified system of records described in this notice includes the following changes.
First, the CFPB is clarifying that the Chief Privacy Officer is the system manager for records related to requests for amendment of records pursuant to the Privacy Act and the Bureau's Privacy Act implementation regulation,
12 CFR 1070.56
.
Second, the authority for maintaining the system is broadened to include the Freedom of Information Act,
5 U.S.C. 552
; the Privacy Act of 1974,
5 U.S.C. 552a
; and the Federal Records Act,
44 U.S.C. 3101
.
Third, the system's purpose is updated to specify that records will be used to process Privacy Act requests to amend records and related subsequent actions, if any.
Fourth, the categories of individuals is modified to clearly include individuals requesting amendment of their records under the Privacy Act.
Fifth, the categories of records is updated to include records pertaining to the processing of requests for amendment of records pursuant to the Privacy Act, and related initial appeals and statements of disagreement, if any.
Sixth, a new routine use is introduced to enable disclosure to the NARA or other Federal agencies conducting records inspections pursuant to the Federal Records Act,
44 U.S.C. 2904
and
2906
.
Seventh, the policies and practices for retention and disposal of records are updated to reflect the NARA-approved records retention schedule.
Eighth, the system location is updated to include the new CFPB address.
Lastly, the CFPB is also making non-substantive revisions to the system of records notice to align with the Office of Management and Budget's template in Circular A-108, “Federal Agency Responsibilities for Review, Reporting, and Publication under the Privacy Act,” appendix II (Dec. 2016).
The report of the revised system of records has been submitted to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the U.S. House of Representatives, the Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs of the U.S. Senate, and the Office of Management and Budget, pursuant to Circular A-108, “Federal Agency Responsibilities for Review, Reporting, and Publication under the Privacy Act” (Dec. 2016) and the Privacy Act of 1974,
5 U.S.C. 552a(r)
. The modified SORN titled, “CFPB.001—Freedom of Information Act/Privacy Act System” is published in its entirety below.
SYSTEM NAME AND NUMBER:
CFPB.001—Freedom of Information Act/Privacy Act System.
SECURITY CLASSIFICATION:
Unclassified.
SYSTEM LOCATION:
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024.
SYSTEM MANAGER(S):
Chief FOIA Officer and Chief Privacy Officer, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024; (855) 444-3642.
AUTHORITY FOR MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM:
5 U.S.C. 552
;
5 U.S.C. 552a
;
12 U.S.C. 5492
,
5493
;
44 U.S.C. 3101
.
PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:
The information in the system is collected to enable the CFPB to carry out certain specific responsibilities under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and Privacy Act of 1974 (Privacy Act). It allows CFPB staff to receive, track, and respond to access requests and initial administrative appeals under the FOIA as well as access and amendment requests and initial appeals under the Privacy Act, including statements of disagreement regarding a request for amendment. The information is also used to gather data to meet statutory FOIA reporting requirements, outlined in
5 U.S.C. 552(e)
, mandating that all Federal agencies compile and submit detailed data to the Attorney General regarding their administration of the law and to manage FOIA-related fees and calculations. The information will also be used for administrative purposes to ensure quality control, performance, and improving management processes.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
Records are maintained on persons requesting access to records pursuant to the FOIA; individuals who have submitted a request for access to or amendment of records pursuant to the Privacy Act; persons or individuals whose information requests are treated as FOIA and/or Privacy Act requests; and persons or individuals filing an administrative appeal of a denial, in whole or part, of any such request. Other individuals covered include Bureau staff assigned to process such requests and related actions to ensure compliance with the FOIA and/or Privacy Act; individuals submitting on the requester's behalf; and personnel of Federal agencies processing consultations and referrals.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
Records in the system may contain: (1) correspondence (
e.g.,
agency acknowledgment letter, access request) from or with the requester or individual submitting on the requester's behalf about the FOIA access requests; Privacy Act access or amendment requests; initial FOIA and/or Privacy Act appeals; and Privacy Act statements of disagreement; (2) documents generated or compiled during the search and processing of the access request for records; (3) fee schedules, cost calculations, and assessed cost for disclosed FOIA and/or PA records; (4) documents and memoranda supporting the decision made in response to the FOIA or PA access request, referral, or consultation, and copies of records provided or withheld; (5) documents and memoranda supporting the decision made in response to the PA amendment requests; (6) documents and memoranda supporting the decision made in response to initial appeals and related actions; (7) identifying information of Bureau staff processing requests and, where a request has been referred to another agency with equities in a responsive document, information about the individual handling the request on behalf of that agency; (8) information identifying the entity that is subject to the requests or appeals; (9) for FOIA access requests, the requester's information, including name, address,
(
printed page 66553)
phone number, email address, FOIA tracking number, phone number, financial payment information, or some combination thereof; (10) for Privacy Act access or amendment requests, information verifying the identity of the individual who is making the written request or appeal, and/or the individual on whose behalf such written requests are made, including name, a photocopy of a single or two forms of identification that bears the requester's photograph and/or signature (
e.g.,
driver's license, or Social Security card and identification with photograph), address, phone number, email address, Bureau-generated record number, phone number, financial payment information (for Privacy Act access requests only), or some combination thereof; (11) records related to inquires or communications submitted to other Federal agencies (
e.g.,
Department of Justice; National Archives and Records Administration, Office of Government Information Services (OGIS)) regarding agency reporting and compliance, and all records related to the resolution of such inquiries.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
Information in this system covers individuals about whom records are maintained; agency staff assigned to help process, consider, and respond to the request, including any appeals; entities filing requests or appeals on behalf of the requestor; other governmental authorities; and entities that are the subjects of the request or appeals.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
In addition to those disclosures generally permitted under
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)
of the Privacy Act, and consistent with the CFPB's Disclosure of Records and Information Rules, promulgated at
12 CFR part 1070
, all or a portion of the records or information contained in this system may be disclosed outside the CFPB as a routine use to:

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is proposing to amend its regulations governing the requirements for federal share insurance. This action would remove the requirement for federally insured, state-chartered credit unions to establish a special reserve for certain investments that are beyond those authorized for federally chartered credit unions. The intended effect is to reduce unnecessary compliance and administrative burdens for state-chartered insured credit unions without diminishing the agency's ability to protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund.
DATES:

Please send comments by one method only
):

.
The docket number for this proposed rule is NCUA-2026-1886. Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions. If you are reading this document on
federalregister.gov,
you may use the green “SUBMIT A PUBLIC COMMENT” button beneath this rulemaking's title to submit a comment to the
regulations.gov
docket. A plain language summary of the proposed rule is also available on the docket website.

to view the public comments. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Introduction
A. Background
Part 741 generally applies to federal credit unions (FCUs), federally insured, state-chartered credit unions (FISCUs), and credit unions applying for insurance of accounts pursuant to Title II of the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act). This part prescribes various requirements for obtaining and maintaining federal share insurance and the payment of insurance premiums and capitalization deposit. Subpart A of part 741 contains substantive requirements that are not codified elsewhere in the NCUA's regulations. Subpart B lists additional regulations that are codified elsewhere in the NCUA's regulations as applying to FCUs, which also apply to FISCUs.
As discussed later in this preamble, the Board is proposing to amend a regulatory requirement in subpart A of part 741 to provide more flexibility and reduce regulatory burden for FISCUs. Section 741.3 requires a FISCU to establish a special reserve for nonconforming investments.
[
1
]
The proposed rule would remove the special reserve requirement.
The Board last amended FISCU special reserve requirements in 1999 when the Board amended the terminology to refer to the special reserve account.
[
2
]
The final rule renamed the accounts “Investment Valuation Reserve Account” and “Investment Valuation Reserve” to “Appropriation for Non-conforming Investments.” The change more appropriately reflected the function and composition of the account under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this proposal pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, the NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for FICUs.
[
3
]
The FCU Act grants the NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
4
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
5
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
6
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the credit union industry and the Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
Additionally, the FCU Act expressly provides that applications for insurance must contain an agreement by the applicant to maintain such special reserves as the Board, by regulation or in special cases, may require for protecting the interest of members.
[
7
]
The Board has exercised its general authority to issue regulations on safe and sound
(
printed page 66533)
banking practices and its authority under the FCU Act to require special reserves under part 741. Part 741 requires a FISCU to establish a special reserve for investments if those credit unions make investments beyond those authorized in the FCU Act or NCUA's rules, and the book value of the investment is over the investment's market value or the market value cannot be determined (nonconforming investments).
II. Proposed Rule
The NCUA has required a special reserve for nonconforming investments since the 1980s.
[
8
]
The NCUA imposes this requirement as some FISCUs are permitted to make investments beyond those authorized in the FCU Act or NCUA regulations for FCUs. As FCU investments generally are limited to relatively conservative instruments, investments outside of those limited investments may carry additional risk and raise safety and soundness concerns.
The Board is now proposing to rescind the requirement for a special reserve related to nonconforming investments. The Board finds the special reserve no longer necessary for safety and soundness because subsequent changes to GAAP have limited the applicability of the reserve requirement. As a practical matter, the special reserve does not provide additional loss absorbing capacity. Also, since the reserve was adopted in the 1980s, GAAP has been amended to require more investments to be carried at fair value instead of book value.
Currently, only seven FISCUs report a special reserve due to a nonconforming investment. Given the current limited applicability, and the fact the special reserve does not actually increase a credit union's loss absorbing capacity, the Board does not believe this provision is necessary for safety and soundness.
The proposed rule would also rescind the cross reference included in § 741.3(a). Section 741.3(a) states that, in determining the insurability of a credit union which makes application for insurance and in continuing the insurability of its accounts pursuant to title II of the FCU Act, FISCUs are subject to statutory prompt corrective action provisions,
[
9
]
its implementing regulation, and subpart L of part 747 of this chapter. These are cross references, and each referenced statute and regulation also states its applicability to FISCUs. Therefore, these references can be removed as duplicative, and the Board proposes to do so.
The proposed rule would also amend a reference to the nonconforming reserve in part 703 of NCUA's regulations (part 703). Section 703.1 sets forth what is included and excluded from part 703. Paragraph (b)(6) excludes FISCU investment activity provided in § 741.3 related to non-conforming investments. The proposed rule would strike this reference.
Additionally, the proposed rule would remove a reference to appropriations for non-conforming investments in the risk-based capital rule. Section 702.104(b) states which elements are included in the definition of risk-based capital. One of the included elements is an appropriation for non-conforming investments.
[
10
]
The proposed rule would remove this reference. The Board notes that under GAAP the special reserve is already considered part of undivided earnings. In removing the special reserve requirement, there should be no prompt corrective action implications from removing the appropriation account. The Board invites comment on this aspect of the proposal.
The Board solicits comments on all aspects of this proposal, but specifically solicits comment on the following:
Question 1. Should the Board consider alternatives to addressing nonconforming investments? For example, instead of a reserve, or addressing safety and soundness risks through the supervisory process, should the Board consider assigning a higher risk weight under part 702 for FICUs subject to risk-based capital requirements?
Question 2: Do commenters believe that the limited number of FISCUs holding nonconforming reserves is due to the disincentive to hold nonconforming investments resulting from the special reserve requirement in part 741? Do commenters expect FISCU investment activity to materially change if the proposed rule is adopted as final?
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023
The Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 (
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
) requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include the internet address of a summary of not more than 100 words in length of a proposed rule, in plain language, that shall be posted on the internet website under section 206(d) of the E-Government Act of 2002 (
44 U.S.C. 3501 note
) (commonly known as
regulations.gov
).
The Board is proposing to amend its regulations governing the requirements for federal share insurance. This action would remove the requirement for FISCUs to establish a special reserve for certain investments that are beyond those authorized for FCUs. The intended effect is to reduce unnecessary compliance and administrative burdens for FISCUs without diminishing the agency's ability to protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund.
The proposal and the required summary can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
11
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
12
]
This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this proposed rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
13
]
This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
14
]
generally requires an agency to conduct
(
printed page 66534)
a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
15
]
For purposes of this analysis, the NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
16
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
The proposed rule would remove a requirement for a separate reserve account. FISCUs would no longer need to account for the reserve or hold capital related to certain nonconforming investments. As described previously, the Board believes that the current requirement has a limited impact. Thus, it does not believe its removal would have a significant effect. Accordingly, the Board certifies the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the change in the proposed rule does not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests. The NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. This proposed rule would apply to all FISCUs and would remove a separate requirement imposed only on FISCUs. There would be no effect on states or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. To the extent that the proposed rule would affect FISCUs uniquely, it would tend to remove a requirement that applies solely to FISCUs and would eliminate a burden that may apply based on their status and activity as state-chartered credit unions. The NCUA welcomes comments on ways to eliminate, or at least minimize, any potential impact in this area.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The NCUA has determined that this proposed rule would not affect family well-being within the meaning of section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
17
]
The proposed rule relates to special reserves held by FISCUs for certain investments, and any effect on family well-being is expected to be indirect.

The NCUA Board (Board) solicits public comment on a proposal to remove a regulatory provision regarding the process for maintaining federal share insurance following the conversion of a federal credit union (FCU) to a state charter. The provision is unnecessarily duplicative of a similar provision contained in NCUA's Chartering and Field of Membership Manual (Manual), and is outdated, having been superseded by amendments to the Manual.

Comments must be received by December 21, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
On October 23, 1986, NCUA published a final rule amending its regulations in
12 CFR part 741
, setting forth the requirements for obtaining and maintaining federal share insurance by credit unions.
[
1
]
Among other amendments, the October 23, 1986, final rule established regulations governing the maintenance of share insurance by an FCU converting to a state charter. This regulation, currently located in § 741.7, provides that an FCU “that petitions to convert to a state-chartered federally insured credit union is required to apply to the NCUA Regional Director for continued insurance of its accounts.”
[
2
]
On December 2, 2008, NCUA published a final rule to codify the Manual as Appendix B to the regulations in
12 CFR part 701
(captioned—“Organization and Operation of Federal Credit Unions”).
[
3
]
Chapter 4 of the Manual governs charter conversions generally, and section III of that chapter specifically addresses the conversion of an FCU to a state charter. As originally enacted, chapter 4, section III of the Manual tracked the wording of § 741.7 by providing that regional director approval was required for the continuation of federal share insurance subsequent to such conversion. Specifically, former chapter 4, section III.B. of the Manual provided that if “the [FCU] intends to continue federal share insurance after the conversion to a state credit union, it must submit an Application for Insurance of Accounts (NCUA 9600) to the regional director at the time it requests approval of the conversion proposal.”
[
4
]
NCUA has twice amended chapter 4, section III.B. of the Manual since its regulatory codification in 2008. These amendments have been prompted by NCUA organizational changes in how the agency carries out its functions and responsibilities. On December 7, 2016, NCUA published a final rule that, among other changes, transferred responsibility for approving continued share insurance following an FCU conversion to the NCUA Office of Consumer Financial Protection and Access.
[
5
]
Another final rule was published on December 20, 2017, to reflect further NCUA reorganization.
[
6
]
This final rule transferred approval authority to NCUA's Office of Credit Union Resources and Expansion (CURE).
NCUA inadvertently failed to make conforming changes to § 741.7 as part of the 2016 and 2017 final rules. As a result, § 741.7 has been effectively superseded by these amendments to the Manual. The regulation is outdated, referring to a process for the approval of continued share insurance following an FCU's conversion that is no longer applicable. To address these concerns, NCUA proposes to remove § 741.7.
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this proposed rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act.
[
7
]
Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs). The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
8
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to NCUA to issue regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
9
]
II. Proposed Rule
The proposed removal of § 741.7 would address several concerns. As discussed, the provision is outdated, having been superseded by the changes made to the Manual. An FCU wishing to retain federal share insurance after converting to a state charter is no longer required to seek approval from the regional director, as provided in § 741.7, but must instead submit its request to CURE. The removal of § 741.7 would help ensure that NCUA's regulations are up-to-date and eliminate potential confusion regarding the approval process for continued share insurance following an FCU's conversion.
In addition, the fact that the Manual and § 741.7 address the same issue is reflective of the fact that, prior to 2008, the Manual was not codified in the Code of Federal Regulations. However, upon the regulatory codification of the Manual, the two provisions became unnecessarily duplicative. As exemplified by § 741.7, such duplication runs the risk of an inadvertent inconsistency being introduced when one of the provisions is amended and a conforming change is not made to the other. The removal of § 741.7 would eliminate this redundancy and the possibility of additional inconsistencies being created in the regulations.
NCUA emphasizes the technical, non-substantive nature of the proposed regulatory change. The proposed rule would not amend the existing process for an FCU seeking to maintain share insurance following its conversion to a state charter. Such process will continue to be governed by chapter 4 of the Manual.
(
printed page 66536)
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023
The Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 (
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
) (Act) requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include the internet address of a summary of not more than 100 words in length of a proposed rule, in plain language, that shall be posted on the internet website under section 206(d) of the E-Government Act of 2002 (
44 U.S.C. 3501 note
) (commonly known as
regulations.gov
).
In summary, the Board solicits public comment on a proposal to remove a regulatory provision regarding the process for maintaining federal share insurance following the conversion of an FCU to a state charter. The provision is unnecessarily duplicative of a similar provision contained in the Manual, and is outdated, having been superseded by amendments to the Manual.
The proposal and the required summary can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
10
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
11
]
This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this proposed rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
12
]
This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This proposed rule is expected to be an
Executive Order 14912
deregulatory action.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
13
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
14
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
15
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
The proposed rule is exclusively concerned with the removal of the obsolete § 741.7, which has been superseded by amendments made to the Manual. The proposal would not make any substantive changes to existing regulatory requirements. To the extent the proposed rule has any economic effect, it would be to relieve credit unions of the costs borne in attempting to reconcile apparently contradictory regulatory provisions. Any such costs are likely minimal. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. NCUA has determined that the changes in the proposed rule do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
16
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. While the scope of the proposal involves FCUs converting to a state charter, the proposed rule would not alter existing requirements governing such conversions. As noted, the proposed rule is exclusively concerned with the removal of an obsolete regulatory provision. Therefore, to the extent the proposed would have any impact on credit unions, it would be to provide greater clarity regarding the applicable requirements governing conversion to a state charter. The proposed rule would not have a substantial direct effect on the states, the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. NCUA welcomes comments on ways to eliminate, or at least minimize, any potential impact in this area.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
NCUA has determined that this proposed rule would not affect family well-being within the meaning of section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
17
]
As noted, the proposed rule removes an outdated regulatory provision that has been superseded by subsequent amendments to other codified provisions. The potential positive effect on family well-being, including financial well-being is, at most, indirect.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Proposed rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
NMFS proposes two technical revisions to regulations for the opening and closing times of groundfish fisheries in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands (BSAI) and Gulf of Alaska (GOA) management areas. First, this proposed rule would authorize NMFS to determine the opening and closing times for the sablefish Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) and Community Development Quota (CDQ) fishing season, taking into consideration the halibut IFQ/CDQ season set by the International Pacific Halibut Commission (IPHC). Second, this proposed rule would allow NMFS flexibility to change the time of day for closing a groundfish fishery. This proposed rule is necessary to minimize regulatory discards, reduce uncertainty for fishery participants, and enable fuller utilization and more precise limitation of allowable harvest. This action is intended to promote the goals and objectives of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act), the Fishery Management Plan for the Groundfish of the BSAI Management Area (BSAI FMP) and the Fishery Management Plan for the Groundfish Fisheries of the GOA (GOA FMP), and other applicable laws.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for Action
NMFS manages the groundfish fisheries in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) under the BSAI FMP and GOA FMP. The North Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council) prepared and recommended these FMPs under the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Act,
16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.
Regulations governing U.S. fisheries and implementing the BSAI and GOA FMPs appear at
50 CFR parts 600
and
679
. This action is necessary to effectively carry out section 3.5.1 (Fishing Seasons) of both the BSAI FMP and GOA FMP, which defines when harvesting groundfish is permitted. That section of both FMPs states that the Secretary of Commerce will establish all fishing seasons by regulations that implement the FMPs to accomplish the goals and objectives of the FMPs, the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and other applicable laws.
Background
Section 3.5.1 (Fishing Seasons) of the BSAI and GOA FMPs defines the
(
printed page 66542)
periods when harvesting groundfish is permitted, the criteria the Council uses for recommending regulatory changes to fishing seasons, and the responsibility of the Secretary of Commerce for establishing fishing season by regulations to accomplish the goals and objectives of the FMPs. Groundfish seasons are specified at
50 CFR 679.23
and the authority to implement fishery closures is specified at § 679.20(d). A more detailed description of the background information and need for this proposed rule is provided in the Analysis prepared for this action (see
ADDRESSES
).
Sablefish and Halibut IFQ/CDQ Season Timing
Pacific halibut and sablefish fisheries off Alaska are managed under different statutory authorities, but harvest for both species often occurs at the same time. Pacific halibut fisheries in and off Alaska are managed under the authority of the Northern Pacific Halibut Act of 1982 (Halibut Act), which domestically implements an international agreement between the United States and Canada with annual allocations to each country set by the IPHC. The IPHC annually recommends management regulations that are subject to approval by the Secretary of State with the concurrence of the Secretary of Commerce, and NMFS then publishes the management measures as regulations on behalf of the IPHC. In contrast, sablefish fisheries in the EEZ off Alaska are managed under the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. Although implemented under different authorities, the directed fixed gear commercial sablefish and halibut fisheries in Alaska are managed under the Halibut and Sablefish IFQ Program and the CDQ Program codified at
50 CFR part 679
. Because many fishery participants hold halibut IFQ and sablefish IFQ and fish both simultaneously, they have benefited from aligned season timing.
Historically, the IPHC has set the time of day for the opening and closing of the halibut commercial fishing period as 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), which aligned with the time for the groundfish openings and closures, which includes the sablefish IFQ/CDQ fishing season, that is set in regulation. However, in 2024 the IPHC changed the opening of the halibut season to 0600 hours, A.l.t., and closing to 2359 hours, A.l.t., in response to requests from fishery participants (
89 FR 19275
,
18
March 2024). While the Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) can set the sablefish IFQ/CDQ fishing season dates to align with the commercial halibut IFQ/CDQ fishery for the purposes of reducing bycatch and regulatory discards between the two fisheries (§ 679.23(g)), current regulations direct that the opening and closing time for groundfish, including sablefish, must be 1200 hours, A.l.t. (§ 679.23(b)).
Vessel operators targeting halibut are frequently also targeting and catching sablefish as recognized in the language of § 679.23(g), such that the two fisheries can benefit from shared opening and closing times. A mismatch in opening and closing times for the sablefish and halibut IFQ/CDQ fisheries can lead to an increase in sablefish discards. Under current regulation at § 679.20(e), sablefish that are caught in the halibut fishery before 1200 hours, A.l.t., of the opening day or after 1200 hours, A.l.t., of the closing day cannot be retained over the maximum retainable amount (MRA) because they are counted as incidental catch. This requires sablefish and halibut IFQ/CDQ harvesters to either delay setting gear for halibut or discard sablefish caught in excess of the MRA for the first 6 hours of the halibut season and the last 12 hours of the halibut season.
Groundfish Closure Timing
Current regulations require the time for all openings and closures of groundfish fishing seasons, other than the beginning and end of the calendar fishing year, be set at 1200 hours, A.l.t. (§ 679.23(b)). If the Regional Administrator determines that a groundfish fishery opening or closure is warranted under § 679.20(d), NMFS announces the opening or closure in the
Federal Register
. Although NMFS specifies the time of these openings and closures, currently § 679.23(b) requires that the time specified always be 1200 hours, A.l.t. The fixed time of 1200 hours, A.l.t., sometimes results in NMFS closing a fishery under § 679.20(d) before the total allowable catch (TAC) is fully harvested. For example, if NMFS determines that the fishing fleet is catching 500 metric tons (mt) of groundfish every 24 hours and there is 750 mt remaining, NMFS must close the fishery at 1200 hours, A.l.t., the day before the TAC is reached, resulting in a 250 mt underage of TAC. Under this same scenario, given more flexibility on the closing time than is currently permitted, NMFS could close the fishery at 2400 hours, A.l.t., which would allow for more of the remaining 250 mt of groundfish to be harvested and could allow the TAC to be fully utilized while still avoiding a TAC overage.
Need for This Action
Current regulations at § 679.23(b) do not provide flexibility for NMFS to determine the best time of day to open or close a groundfish fishery.
In April 2025, the Council requested that NMFS revise regulations to allow NMFS to align the sablefish IFQ/CDQ season timing with the fishing period the IPHC sets for the commercial halibut IFQ/CDQ fishery. This action would minimize regulatory discards, improve harvest efficiency, and reduce uncertainty for fishery participants. Giving NMFS the flexibility to align the opening and closing times for sablefish and halibut IFQ/CDQ fishing seasons will ensure that sablefish IFQ/CDQ holders do not need to discard sablefish for the first 6 hours or the last 12 hours of the halibut IFQ/CDQ fishing season. In addition, should the IPHC revise the opening and closing time for the commercial halibut IFQ/CDQ fishery in the future, NMFS would have the ability to follow suit.
In October 2025, the Council expressed support for NMFS to modify the groundfish fishery closure timing to allow NMFS the flexibility to close the fishery at a different time if necessary for harvest to be closer to the TAC. This action would allow the Regional Administrator to close a groundfish fishery at a different time of the day, giving NMFS more flexibility and potentially allowing groundfish TACs to be more fully utilized and to avoid TAC overages. This would result in greater precision of management of some groundfish fisheries and reduce the probability of falling short of the TAC for the groundfish fleets. By allowing NMFS to specify the appropriate closure time instead of defaulting to 1200 hours, A.l.t., vessel operators may have additional opportunity to harvest and maximize the catch of valuable groundfish due to additional fishing hours. In addition, NMFS would have more flexibility in setting a closure time that ensures a TAC is not exceeded.
Proposed Rule
Through this action, NMFS is proposing to do the following: (1) modify regulations to allow the Regional Administrator to determine the opening and closing times of the sablefish IFQ/CDQ season based on dates and times for the halibut season, and (2) modify regulations to allow the Regional Administrator the flexibility to set the time of day for a groundfish closure when NMFS takes an inseason management action under § 679.20(d).
(
printed page 66543)
Sablefish IFQ/CDQ Season Timing
The first revision to address sablefish season timing alignment would apply exclusively to vessel operators fishing for sablefish under the IFQ and CDQ Programs with fixed gear in the BSAI and GOA management areas and would authorize the Regional Administrator to determine the opening and closing times for the sablefish IFQ/CDQ fishing season, taking into consideration the halibut IFQ/CDQ season set by the IPHC. To accomplish this, the proposed rule would revise § 679.23(g)(1) to allow the Regional Administrator to set the season opening and closing times by amending to state “opening and closing dates and times for sablefish” where originally the Regional Administrator only determined the opening date for sablefish. An exception from the 1200 hours, A.l.t., for sablefish IFQ/CDQ opening and closing time would also be added by new § 679.23(b)(1) because currently § 679.23(b) sets the opening and closing time of groundfish fisheries at 1200 hours, A.l.t., and sablefish is a groundfish (Table 2a to
50 CFR part 679.2
).
Groundfish Season Closures
The second revision would allow NMFS flexibility in inseason closures to specify the time of day for closing groundfish fisheries, which is currently set at 1200 hours, A.l.t., and these inseason closures would apply to all vessel operators fishing groundfish in the BSAI and GOA management areas. To accomplish this, the proposed rule would add § 679.23(b)(2) to provide that the time of all groundfish closures of fishing seasons is 1200 hours, A.l.t., unless NMFS establishes a different fishery closure time in an action taken under § 679.20(d). Actions that NMFS may take under § 679.20(d), where NMFS may set a different time than 1200 hours A.l.t., include: (1) prohibiting directed fishing when a directed fishing allowance has been or will be reached (§ 679.20(d)(1)(iii)), (2) modifying any applicable side board limit once the sideboard directed fishing allowance is or will be reached (§ 679.20(d)(1)(iv), (v)), and (3) requiring that a groundfish species be treated in the same manner as prohibited species catch to avoid exceeding a TAC (
i.e.,
no retention allowed) (§ 679.20(d)(2)). The Regional Administrator may also establish area closures under § 679.25; however, these provisions are rarely used and there is no projected benefit to giving NMFS flexibility to set § 679.25 closures at a time other than 1200 hours, A.l.t. Therefore, NMFS is proposing limiting this change to inseason actions taken under § 679.20(d) only.
Classification
NMFS is proposing this rule pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is taken to effectively set season opening and closing timing pursuant to section 3.5.1 of both the BSAI and GOA FMPs. The NMFS Assistant Administrator has determined that this proposed rule is consistent with the BSAI and GOA FMPs and is consistent with other applicable law, subject to further consideration after public comment.
This proposed rule has been determined to be not significant for the purposes of
Executive Order 12866
.
Certification Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Senior Lead Counsel for Regulation of the Department of Commerce certified to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration that this proposed rule, if adopted, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. NMFS requests comments on this certification for this proposed rule. The factual basis for this determination is as follows.
This proposed rule would minimize regulatory burden on vessel operators that participate in the sablefish IFQ/CDQ fisheries and allow for increased predictability of season timing. This proposed action would also allow groundfish closures based on inseason management actions that could reduce the probability of entities either exceeding or falling short of the TAC. As a result, this proposed action would not have any adverse economic impacts on the small directly regulated entities, and the beneficial economic impact would likely be modest and not significant.
In the BSAI area, there were 92 individual catcher vessels (CVs) and 1 catcher/processor (C/P) with gross revenues less than or equal to $11 million, based on the most recent year of data (2024). The six CDQ groups are also considered small entities. This represents the potential suite of directly regulated small entities. The determination of entity size is based on vessel revenues and affiliated group revenues. This determination also includes an assessment of fisheries cooperative affiliations, although actual vessel ownership affiliations have not been completely established. However, the estimate of these 93 vessels may be an overstatement of the number of small entities because of the complexity of analyzing the links and affiliations across these vessels, particularly since many of them conduct operations in both Federal and State fisheries. There are 3 American Fisheries Act (AFA) cooperative affiliated motherships that appear to fall under the 750 worker threshold and are therefore small entities.
In the GOA area, there were 602 individual CV and C/P entities with gross revenues less than or equal to $11 million, based on the most recent year of complete data (2024). This includes an estimated 601 small CV entities and one small C/P entity in the GOA groundfish sector. The determination of entity size is based on vessel revenues and affiliated group revenues. This determination also includes an assessment of fisheries cooperative affiliations, although actual vessel ownership affiliations have not been completely established. However, the estimate of these 602 CVs and C/Ps may be an overstatement of the number of small entities because of the complexity of analyzing the links and affiliations across these vessels, particularly since many of them conduct operations in both Federal and State fisheries.
For the reasons described above, this action is expected to be beneficial by reducing regulatory discards and uncertainty for sablefish IFQ/CDQ harvesters and reducing the probability of falling short of the TAC for the groundfish fleets. This action is administrative and will not negatively impact the amount or location of harvest under any of the fishery management programs affected by this action. Total economic impacts are not expected to be significant as it will simplify and clarify regulations on the time of the day that sablefish seasons may open and close and the time of day that groundfish seasons may close, allowing more predictability for sablefish IFQ/CDQ harvesters and more efficient utilization of TAC for actions under § 679.20(d).
This proposed action, therefore, is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. As a result, an initial regulatory flexibility analysis is not required, and none has been prepared.

AGENCY:
State Justice Institute.
ACTION:
Grant guideline for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027.
SUMMARY:
This guideline sets forth the administrative, programmatic, and financial requirements attendant to FY 2027 State Justice Institute grants.
DATES:
October 19, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
State Justice Institute, 12700 Fair Lakes Circle, Suite 340, Fairfax, VA 22033.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jonathan Mattiello, Executive Director, State Justice Institute, 703-660-4979,
jonathan.mattiello@sji.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Pursuant to the State Justice Institute Act of 1984 (
42 U.S.C. 10701
et seq.
), the State Justice Institute is authorized to award grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts to State and local courts, nonprofit organizations, and others for the purpose of improving the quality of justice in the State courts of the United States.
The following Grant Guideline is adopted by the State Justice Institute for FY 2027.
Table of Contents
I. Eligibility
II. Grant Application Deadlines
III. The Mission of the State Justice Institute
IV. Grant Types
V. Application and Submission Information
VI. How To Apply
VII. Postaward Reporting Requirements
VIII. Compliance Requirements
IX. Financial Requirements
X. Grant Adjustments
I. Eligibility
Pursuant to the State Justice Institute Act of 1984 (
42 U.S.C. 10701
et seq.
), the State Justice Institute (SJI) is authorized to award grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts to State and local courts, national nonprofit organizations, and others for the purpose of improving the quality of justice in the State courts of the United States.
SJI is authorized by Congress to award grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts to the following entities and types of organizations:
State and local courts and their agencies (
42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(1)(A)
).
National nonprofit organizations controlled by, operating in conjunction with, and serving the judicial branches of State governments (
42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(1)(B)
).
National nonprofit organizations for the education and training of judges and support personnel of the judicial branch of State governments (
42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(1)(C)
). An applicant is considered a national education and training applicant under section 10705(b)(1)(C) if:
the principal purpose or activity of the applicant is to provide education and training to State and local judges and court personnel, and
the applicant demonstrates a record of substantial experience in the field of judicial education and training.
Other eligible grant recipients (
42 U.S.C. 10705
(b)(2)(A) through (D)).
Provided that the objectives of the project can be served better, SJI is also authorized to make awards to:
nonprofit organizations with expertise in judicial administration;
institutions of higher education;
individuals, partnerships, firms, and corporations (for-profit organizations must waive their fees); and
private agencies with expertise in judicial administration.
SJI may also make awards to State or local agencies and institutions other than courts for services that cannot be adequately provided through nongovernmental arrangements (
42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(3)
).
SJI is prohibited from awarding grants to Federal, tribal, and international courts.
II. Grant Application Deadlines
The SJI Board of Directors makes awards on a quarterly basis aligned with the Federal fiscal year. Applications may be submitted at any time but will be considered for award based only on the timetable below.
Table 1—Application Deadlines by Federal Fiscal Year Quarter
Federal fiscal year quarter
Application
                             due date
1
November 1.
2
February 1.
3
May 1.
4
August 1.
To be considered timely, an application must be submitted by the application deadline noted above. Applicants must use the SJI Grants Management System (GMS) to submit all applications and postaward documents. The SJI GMS is accessible at
https://gms.sji.gov
. SJI urges applicants to submit applications at least 72 hours prior to the application due date to allow time for the applicant to receive an application acceptance message and to correct in a timely fashion any problems that may arise, such as missing or incomplete forms.
Questions related to the SJI Grant Program or the SJI GMS should be directed to
contact@sji.gov
.
III. The Mission of the State Justice Institute
The State Justice Institute Act of 1984 (
42 U.S.C. 10701
et seq.
) established SJI to improve the administration of justice in the State courts of the United States. Incorporated in the State of Virginia as a private, nonprofit corporation, SJI is charged, by statute, with the responsibility to:
direct a national program of financial assistance designed to ensure that each citizen of the United States is provided ready access to a fair and effective system of justice,
foster coordination and cooperation with the Federal judiciary,
promote recognition of the importance of the separation-of-powers
(
printed page 66600)
doctrine to an independent judiciary, and
encourage education for judges and support personnel of State court systems through national and State organizations.
To accomplish these broad objectives, SJI is authorized to provide funding to State courts, national organizations that support and are supported by State courts, national judicial education organizations, and other organizations that can assist in improving the quality of justice in the State courts.
Through the award of grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements, SJI is authorized to perform the following activities:
support technical assistance, demonstrations, special projects, research, and training to improve the administration of justice in the State courts;
provide for the preparation, publication, and dissemination of information regarding State judicial systems;
participate in joint projects with Federal agencies and other private grantors;
evaluate or provide for the evaluation of programs and projects to determine their impact upon the quality of criminal, civil, and juvenile justice and the extent to which they have contributed to improving the quality of justice in the State courts;
encourage and assist in furthering judicial education; and
encourage, assist, and serve in a consulting capacity State and local courts in the development, maintenance, and coordination of criminal, civil, and juvenile justice programs and services.
SJI is supervised by a board of directors appointed by the U.S. President, with the advice and consent of the U.S. Senate. The SJI Board of Directors is statutorily composed of six judges, a State court administrator, and four members of the public, no more than two of whom may belong to the same political party. Additional information about SJI, including a list of members of the SJI Board of Directors, is available at
https://www.sji.gov
.
a. Priority Investment Areas
The SJI Board of Directors has established Priority Investment Areas for grant funding. SJI will allocate significant financial resources through grants for these Priority Investment Areas. The Priority Investment Areas are applicable to all grant types. SJI strongly encourages potential grant applicants to consider projects addressing one or more of these Priority Investment Areas and to integrate the following factors into each proposed project:
evidence-based, data-driven decision making;
cross-sector collaboration;
systemic approaches (as opposed to standalone programs);
institutionalization of new court processes and procedures;
ease of replication; and
sustainability.
For FY 2027, the Priority Investment Areas are listed below in no specific order.
1. Opioids and Other Dangerous Drugs and Behavioral Health Responses
Opioids and Behavioral Health Court Responses
—Research indicates that justice-involved persons have significantly greater proportions of mental, substance-use, and cooccurring disorders than are found in the general public. SJI supports cross-sector collaboration and information sharing that emphasize policies and practices designed to improve court responses to justice-involved persons with behavioral health and other cooccurring needs.
Trauma-Informed Approaches
—Judges, court staff, system stakeholders, and court-involved persons (
e.g.
, defendants, respondents, and victims) alike may be impacted by prior trauma. This is particularly, but not exclusively, true for those with mental illness and/or substance-use disorders. SJI supports trauma-informed training, policies, and practices in all aspects of the judicial process.
Due to limited grant resources, SJI will not support grants that propose to maintain, enhance, or expand the operations of problem-solving courts. SJI will continue to prioritize innovative projects that can be replicated across the United States regardless of court type. SJI encourages potential applicants to consider Federal grant funding for these activities. Information regarding other funding opportunities is available on SJI's Funding Toolkit, the U.S. Department of Justice's Office of Justice Programs Current Funding Opportunities page, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration Grants Dashboard.
2. Promoting Access to Justice and Procedural Fairness
Procedural Fairness
—A fundamental role of courts is to ensure fair processes and just outcomes for litigants. SJI promotes the integration of research-based procedural-fairness principles, policies, and practices into State court operations to increase public trust and confidence in the court system, reduce recidivism, and increase compliance with court orders.
Self-Represented Litigation
—SJI promotes court-based solutions to address increases in self-represented litigants; helps make courts more user-friendly by simplifying court forms; provides one-on-one assistance; develops guides, handbooks, and instructions on how to proceed; develops court-based self-help centers; and uses internet technologies to increase access. These projects are improving outcomes for litigants and saving valuable court resources.
3. Protecting Victims, Underserved Populations, and Vulnerable Populations
Human Trafficking
—SJI addresses the impact of Federal and State human-trafficking laws on the State courts and the challenges faced by State courts in dealing with cases involving trafficking victims and their families, including victims who are U.S. citizens. These efforts are intended to empower State courts to identify victims, link them with vital services, and hold traffickers accountable.
Rural Justice
—Rural areas and their justice systems routinely have fewer resources and more barriers—such as unavailability of services, lack of transportation, and smaller workforces—than their urban counterparts. Programs and practices that are effective in urban areas are often inappropriate and/or lack research supporting their implementation in rural areas. SJI supports rural courts by identifying promising and best practices and promoting resources, education, and training opportunities that are uniquely designed for rural courts and court users.
Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Elder Issues
—SJI assists courts in improving court oversight of guardians and conservators for the elderly and incapacitated adults through visitor programs, electronic reporting, and training.
4. Advancing Justice Reform
Criminal Justice Reform
—SJI assists State courts in promoting offender accountability and oversight; fostering transparency, governance, and structural reforms that promote access to justice; and implementing innovative diversion and reentry programs that serve to improve outcomes for justice-involved persons and reduce the impact of the costs of the justice system.
Juvenile Justice Reform
—SJI supports innovative projects that
(
printed page 66601)
