ACTION:
Notice of intent to establish a Federal Advisory Committee.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC or Commission) is publishing this notice to announce the intent to establish of 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Federal Advisory Committee (FAC). The Commission has determined that establishing the Committee is necessary and in the public interest.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brian Marenco, Designated Federal Officer, Federal Communications Commission, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, (202) 418-0838, or email:
Brian.Marenco@fcc.gov
;
or Logan Bennett, Deputy Designated Federal Officer, Federal Communications Commission, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, (202) 418-7790 or email:
Logan.Bennett@fcc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with section 9(a)(2) of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA),
5 U.S.C. 1008
, and
41 CFR 102-3.60(a)
, 102-3.65, and 102-3.35, the Commission is announcing the intent to establish the 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Committee (4.9 GHz Committee) and providing herein the Commission-approved public interest determination. The 4.9 GHz Committee's objectives and scope of activities are to provide the Commission with advice and recommendations on the selection of a 4.9 GHz Band Manager to coordinate operations in the 4.9 GHz band (4940-4990 MHz) through optimizing public safety use, facilitating the integration of the latest commercially available technologies and benefitting public safety users. The 4.9 GHz Committee will receive and review proposals from persons or entities seeking to serve as Band Manager and to hold the Band Manager overlay license. The 4.9 GHz Committee will operate for no more than one year from the date of establishment unless the Commission directs that it terminate on an earlier date. A copy of the charter will be posted on the Agency's website at
www.fcc.gov
.
Public Interest Determination
Pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.60(a)
, to establish, renew, reestablish, or merge a discretionary (agency discretion) advisory committee, an agency must first consult with the General Services Administration's Committee Management Secretariat (the Secretariat) and, as part of the consultation, provide a written public interest determination approved by the head of the agency to the Secretariat with a copy to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). In addition, pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.35
, an agency shall follow the same consultation process and document in writing the same determination of need before creating a subcommittee under a discretionary committee that is not made up entirely of members of a parent advisory committee. The Commission provides the following information to demonstrate that establishing the 4.9 GHz Committee is in the public interest:
1.
Annual budget:
The estimated annual operating cost for supporting the 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Committee is $406,822.44.
a.
Federal personnel on a full-time equivalent (FTE) basis:
$350,709 (annual salary of two full-time employees).
b.
Other Federal internal costs:
Additional 16% ($56,113.44).
c.
Proposed payments to members:
Members will not be compensated.
d.
Proposed number of members:
A minimum of seven members.
e.
Reimbursable costs:
$0.
2.
If applicable, the total dollar value of grants expected to be recommended during the fiscal year:
N/A.
3.
Criteria for selecting members to ensure the 4.9 GHz Committee has the necessary expertise and fairly balanced membership:
The FCC envisioned in the Seventh R&O in WP Docket No. 07-100 (38 FCC Rcd at 712, para. 21) that the Band Manager would be recommended by a selection committee “that represents and ensures the involvement of the relevant stakeholders, in particular the public safety community.” The Commission in the Eighth R&O in WP Docket No. 07-100 (39 FCC Rcd at 12066, para. 52) also delegated “broad authority” to the Public Safety and Homeland Security and Wireless Telecommunications Bureaus “to establish the procedures by which a selection committee will be chosen, identify representatives to sit on the selection committee, determine the requisite number of selection committee members, identify the applicable selection criteria, and establish the appropriate procedures and appropriate oversight for the selection process as part of choosing the Band Manager.”
4.
List of all other Federal advisory committees of the Agency:
In addition to the proposed 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Committee, the FCC has four FACA Committees:
a. Communications Security, Reliability and Interoperability Council
b. Consumer Protection and Accessibility Advisory Committee
c. Technological Advisory Council
d. World Radiocommunication Conference Advisory Committee
5.
Justification that the information or advice provided by the committee or subcommittee is not available from another Federal advisory committee, another Federal Government source, or any other more cost-effective and less burdensome source:
The FCC regulates interstate and international communications by radio, television, wire, satellite, and cable in all 50 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories. The Commission is a U.S. government agency overseen by Congress and is the federal agency responsible for implementing and enforcing America's communications law and regulations. Specifically, in its
(
printed page 66559)
work facing economic opportunities and challenges associated with rapidly evolving advances in global communications, the agency capitalizes on its competencies in: promoting competition, innovation and investment in broadband services and facilities, supporting the nation's economy by ensuring an appropriate competitive framework for the unfolding of the communications revolution, encouraging the highest and best use of spectrum domestically and internationally, revising media regulations so that new technologies flourish alongside diversity and localism, and providing leadership in strengthening the defense of the nation's communications infrastructure. The Band Manager selection requires a committee whose sole focus is for carrying out the selection process. The 4.9 GHz Committee will receive and review proposals, select proposals, and make recommendations in line with particular functions appropriate for a Band Manager. The 4.9 GHz Committee is the most cost-effective way to complete this task, particularly since the Commission does not compensate members and does not provide for members' travel expenses and accommodation for meetings. Additionally, the FAC will use minimal employees and only account for a small portion of those employees' overall responsibilities.
6.
If this is a renewal or reestablishment, summarize the committee's previous accomplishments and the reasons it needs to continue:
N/A. This is to establish a new FAC.
7.
Explanation of why the committee/subcommittee is essential to the conduct of Agency business:
The 4.9 GHz Committee shall support the mission of the Commission to make available for all people of the U.S. a rapid, efficient, nationwide, and worldwide wire and radio communication service at reasonable charges through the advisement on the selection of a Band Manager for the 4.9 GHz band by ensuring the person[s] or entity it believes is best suited to perform the Band Manager role is recommended to the Commission through particular criteria and oversight. The 4.9 GHz Committee's responsibility to receive and review proposals for persons or entities to serve as the Band Manager is essential since, once selected, the Band Manger will be eligible to apply for a nationwide overlay license and authorized to enter into a sharing agreement with the First Responder Network Authority (FirstNet). This 4.9 GHz Committee will focus on the following functions: facilitating frequency coordination and interference protection for 4.9 GHz band incumbent public safety operations, including working with incumbent licensees to optimize their spectrum use; developing a spectrum plan for, among other things, incentivizing the use of the latest commercially available technologies, including 5G; entering into and managing a sharing agreement with FirstNet, or similar network, pursuant to §§ 90.1207(h) and 2.103(b) of the Commission's rules; mediating disputes between 4.9 GHz licensees or between licensees and FirstNet, developing and maintaining a plan to maintain the financial viability of the Band Manager; and filing an annual report with the Commission.
In conclusion, this public interest determination documents that establishing the 4.9 GHz Committee is in the public interest, essential to the conduct of FCC business, and that the information to be obtained is not already available through another advisory committee or source within the Federal Government.

Abstract:
Order 12862 directs Federal agencies to provide service to the public that matches or exceeds the best service available in the private sector. In order to work continuously to ensure that our programs are effective and meet our customers' needs, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) seeks to obtain OMB approval of a generic clearance to collect qualitative feedback on our service delivery for Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA); Veterans Health Administration (VHA); and National Cemetery Administration (NCA). By qualitative feedback, we mean information that provides useful insights on perceptions and opinions, but not statistical surveys that yield quantitative results that can be generalized to the population of study.
The proposed information collection activity provides a means to garner qualitative customer and stakeholder feedback in an efficient, timely manner, in accordance with the Administration's commitment to improving service delivery. This feedback will provide insights into customer or stakeholder perceptions, experiences and expectations, provide an early warning of issues with service, or focus attention on areas where communication, training, or changes in operations might improve delivery of products or services. These collections will allow for ongoing, collaborative, and actionable communications between the VA and its customers and stakeholders. They will also provide feedback to contribute directly to the improvement of program management.
The solicitation of feedback will target areas such as timeliness, appropriateness, accuracy of information, courtesy, efficiency of service delivery, and resolution of issues with service delivery. Responses will be assessed to plan and inform efforts to improve or maintain the quality of service offered to the public. If this information is not collected, vital feedback from customers and stakeholders on the provision of services will be unavailable to the Agency.
The Agency will only submit information collections for approval under this generic clearance if they meet the following conditions:
The collections are voluntary;
The collections are low-burden for respondents (based on considerations of total burden hours, total number of respondents, or burden-hours per respondent) and are low-cost for both the respondents and the Federal Government;
The collections are noncontroversial and do not raise issues of concern to other Federal agencies;
Any collection is targeted to the solicitation of opinions from respondents who have experience with the program or may have experience with the program in the near future;
Personally identifiable information (PII) is collected only to the extent necessary and is not retained;
Information gathered will be used only internally for general service improvement and program management purposes and is not intended for release outside of the agency;
Information gathered will not be used for the purpose of substantially informing influential policy decisions; and
Information gathered will yield qualitative information; the collections will not be designed or expected to yield statistically reliable results or used as though the results are generalizable to the population of study.
The types of collections that this generic clearance covers include, but are not limited to, Program Satisfaction Surveys; Focus Groups; Customer Comment Cards; Small Discussion Groups of customers, potential customers, delivery partners, or other stakeholders; Qualitative Customer Satisfaction Surveys, such as post-transaction surveys and opt-out web surveys; In-person Observation Testing, such as website or software usability tests; and Patient Surveys. As a general matter, information collections under this clearance will not result in any new system of records containing privacy information and will not ask questions of a sensitive nature, such as sexual behavior and attitudes, religious beliefs, and other matters that are commonly

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106681; File No. SR-CMESC-2026-011]
October 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 9, 2026, CME Securities Clearing Inc. (“CMESC”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been substantially prepared by CMESC. CMESC filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act.
[
3
]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. CMESC's Statement of the Terms and Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
(a) The proposed rule change of CME Securities Clearing Inc. (“CMESC”) is provided in Exhibit 5. The proposed rule change includes amendments to the CMESC Risk Management Framework (“RMF”) related to CMESC's default management practices, which provides for necessary transparency to and clarity for CMESC staff in managing a default.
[
4
]
Each modification is described in more detail below.
II. CMESC's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, CMESC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. CMESC has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. CMESC's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
Background
CMESC's default management procedures cover the management of a default of either a Member or User (collectively, “Participants”) and are designed to ensure the continuity of CMESC's clearance and settlement functions and particularly, the ongoing maintenance of the services provided to non-defaulting Participants, while supporting market integrity and minimizing market disruptions. The primary purpose of the proposed rule change is to enhance the default management process by further codifying the documentation of the default management procedures in the RMF. In particular, the proposed rule change would amend the RMF to (i) provide additional detail around arrangements involving a third-party liquidation agent for managing a Participant default, and (ii) make certain clarifying and administrative changes, where appropriate, in the RMF; and (iii) to clarify the role of CMESC's Risk Management Committee (“CSRMC”) in designing the default management procedures.
Liquidation Agent and Execution Brokers
Section 14.1.1 (“Participant Default Management Process”) of the RMF would be amended to specify that the close-out process of a defaulted Participant's portfolio may include the use of a liquidation agent and one or more execution brokers.
[
5
]
Broadly, the amended RMF would provide that, in managing a default, CMESC and any liquidation agent will collaborate to assess the exposures of the defaulted Participant's portfolio, including associated settlement obligations as they come due, and formulate a close-out strategy under the prevailing market conditions to minimize potential losses and market disruptions and to support market integrity. More specifically, the amended RMF would describe the expectations for a third-party liquidation agent, if used, to assist CMESC with designing and executing the close-out strategy for the defaulted Participant's portfolio. In accordance with the amended RMF, the liquidation agent will be expected to coordinate with CMESC to reconcile positions of the defaulted Participant and assess the outstanding exposure of the defaulted Participant over the course of managing the default.
The amended RMF also would provide that the liquidation agent may use various methods to execute close-out trades, including, but not limited to, executing open market transactions; enter into hedging transactions to mitigate the risk of the defaulted Participant's portfolio; and perform other related tasks appropriate to assist CMESC in managing the risk from the Participant's default. In addition, Section 14.1.1 of the RMF would recognize that CMESC may engage one or more execution brokers to coordinate with the liquidation agent and CMESC to provide certain operational services related to the close-out trades arranged or executed by the liquidation agent in managing a default. The amended RMF would include new language to specify that, where appropriate, CMESC would maintain an account with the execution broker where it would be the principal, and the execution broker may submit back-to-back trades that mirror the liquidation agent's close-out trades. CMESC would further specify in the RMF that the submission of back-to-back trades is expected to ensure that CMESC's account at the execution broker maintains a net flat position and facilitate CMESC's ability to meet the settlement obligations of the defaulted Participant as they come due.
Clarifying and Administrative Changes
The proposed rule change would also include certain clarifying and administrative changes.
Member Default:
For example, Section 14 (“Default Management”) of the RMF would be amended to clarify that CMESC analyzes Users' risk profile on an
ex ante
basis. The associated monitoring and analysis serves to improve the likelihood that non-defaulted Users' positions can be transferred to a Member in good standing where their authorizing Member has defaulted. Additionally, the RMF would be amended to clarify that, while CMESC makes its best efforts to transfer non-defaulting Users' positions
(
printed page 66588)
(
i.e.,
of a defaulted Member) to non-defaulting Members, CMESC continues to monitor Users' positions and the sufficiency of the associated collateral throughout the default management process and based on the prevailing facts and circumstances may close-out (
e.g.,
liquidate) the positions of some or all Users of a defaulted Member.
User Default:
Section 14.1 (“Participant Default Event”) of the RMF would be updated to specify that an authorizing Member of a defaulted User must respond to CMESC within a period of time prescribed by the Corporation if it wishes to manage the User's default and, if it elects to do so, CMESC will undertake several operational steps relating to the User's positions and collateral to facilitate the Member's management of the User's default in accordance with the CMESC Rules.
[
6
]
Section 14.1 of the RMF would also be amended to include “close-out” in addition to bidding on or purchasing a defaulted Participant's portfolio when gauging Participants' interest prior to declaring another Participant in default.
Additionally, Section 14.1 of the RMF would be amended to clarify that, for Users with multiple authorizing Members, where CMESC manages the User's default, the default management costs will be allocated on a
pro rata
basis based on the margin requirement for the User's positions authorized by each such Member. Moreover, Section 14.1 would be amended to add that the trades of the Users that are expected to settle on the next day after the day of the Member's default may settle prior to the transfer of any other positions.
Participant Default, Generally:
The amended RMF also clarifies certain operational steps CMESC would take if it were to manage a default of a Participant itself. Section 14.1.1 of the amended RMF would provide that CMESC will take appropriate operational steps, as soon as practicable, to contain risk and prevent any unauthorized movement of the default Participant's cash or securities. These operational steps may include appropriate coordination with defaulted Participant's designated Bank(s) and Securities Settlement Bank(s), including enabling CMESC to assume control over outstanding positions and collateral of the defaulter. CMESC will also assess the risk of the defaulted Participant's portfolio, including the maturity of positions and timing for when associated obligations come due. Based on this assessment, CMESC would determine the best strategy for managing the Participant default in order to meet the obligations of the defaulted Participant's portfolio as they arise, including the process for closing out the portfolio and, where necessary, purchasing or selling securities and/or facilitating an auction (or multiple auctions) to meet the settlement obligations of the defaulted Participant.
The proposed changes would also relocate language related to hedging a defaulted Participant's portfolio using futures from 14.1.1.2, which relates generally to CMESC's ability to enter into securities transactions to address a defaulted Participant's settlement obligations, to Section 14.1.1, which describes the Participant default management process generally. In connection with this change, the term “Hedging” is being deleted from the header for Section 14.1.1.2. Additionally, the proposed changes would amend Section 14.1.1.2 to clarify that CMESC would only use its acceleration rights for applicable transactions with remaining maturities of greater than two business days such that non-defaulting Participants' delivery obligations become due on dates earlier than the original maturity dates of such transactions, as is consistent with the terms of existing Rule 1507(f).
[
7
]
Finally, Section 14 would be amended to clarify that CMESC notification of a User default is governed by CMESC's Rules.
[
8
]
CSRMC Role in Designing the Default Management Procedures
Section 14 of the amended RMF specifies that CMESC's Risk Management Committee (“CSRMC”) shall provide guidance to CMESC on the design of its default management procedures, as necessary (
i.e.,
through its ongoing oversight of the RMF).
[
9
]
The current RMF establishes the CSRMC's role in managing a default as discretionary and thus inherently advisory. The proposed amendments clarify the CSRMC's responsibilities prior to and during a default, while preserving its existing power to convene in the latter circumstances.
2. Statutory Basis
For the reasons set forth below, CMESC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
10
]
and SEC Rules 17Ad-22(e)(2)(v),
[
11
]
17Ad-22(e)(3),
[
12
]
17Ad-22(e)(13),
[
13
]
and 17Ad-22(e)(18)(iv)(C)
[
14
]
thereunder.
Consistency With Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act
Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act requires, in part, that the rules of a clearing agency be designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions, to assure the safeguarding of securities and funds which are in the custody or control of the clearing agency or for which it is responsible, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
[
15
]
Robust documentation of default management practices in the RMF, a core component of CMESC's risk management framework, provides the necessary transparency to and clarity for CMESC staff to help facilitate the orderly management of a Participant default. This, in turn, will ensure CMESC continues to clear and settle securities transactions on a prompt and accurate basis and protect the securities and funds of non-defaulting Members despite a Participant default. For these reasons, CMESC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
Consistency With SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(2)(v)
SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(2)(v) requires that a covered clearing agency establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to provide for governance arrangements that specify clear and direct lines of responsibility.
[
16
]
The proposed amendments to Section 14 of the RMF are designed to clarify CSRMC's responsibility in guiding the design of CMESC's default management procedures. As such, CMESC believes that the proposed rule change would further specify the clear and direct lines of responsibility of CSRMC, consistent with SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(2)(v).
(
printed page 66589)
Consistency With SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3)
SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3) requires, in part, that a covered clearing agency establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to maintain a sound risk management framework for comprehensively managing legal, credit, liquidity, operational, general business, investment, custody, and other risks that arise in or are borne by the covered clearing agency, which includes risk management policies, procedures, and systems designed to identify, measure, monitor, and manage the range of risks that arise in or are borne by the covered clearing agency, that are subject to review on a specified periodic basis and approved by the board of directors annually.
[
17
]
The existing RMF is specifically designed to comply with SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3), and the proposed amendments are designed to provide further enhancements and clarity to the manner in which CMESC manages Participant defaults, including potentially through the use of a liquidation agent and execution brokers and the clarifying changes describing CMESC's potential actions during a Participant default, generally, and Member or User defaults, specifically. As such, CMESC believes that the proposed rule change would support a sound, comprehensive framework designed to identify, measure, monitor, and manage the range of risks that arise in or are borne by CMESC, consistent with SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3).
Consistency With SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(13)
SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(13) requires, in part, that a covered clearing agency establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure the covered clearing agency has the authority and operational capacity to take timely action to contain losses and liquidity demands and continue to meet its obligations.
[
18
]
The proposed amendments to the RMF are designed to enhance CMESC's default management process by further documenting CMESC's default management procedures. Having well documented procedures, in turn, will bolster CMESC's rule-based authority and provide further clarity regarding operational steps to contain losses and liquidity demands and continue to meet its obligations, despite a Participant default. Furthermore, the proposed amendments to the RMF would document arrangements with a potential third-party liquidation agent and clarify the default management process involving such a third-party, which if used, could facilitate CMESC's ability to take timely action to close out a defaulting Participant's positions. Therefore, CMESC believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(13).
Consistency With Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18)(iv)(C)
SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18)(iv)(C) requires, in part, that a covered clearing agency establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to establish objective, risk-based, and publicly disclosed criteria for participation, which, when the covered clearing agency provides central counterparty services for transactions in U.S. Treasury securities, ensure that it has appropriate means to facilitate access to the clearance and settlement services of all eligible secondary market transactions in U.S. Treasury securities, including those of indirect participants.
[
19
]
The clarifying changes to the procedures for a Member default are designed to document CMESC's planned efforts, both ex ante and ex post, to increase the probability that a User continues to maintain access to CMESC's services, despite its authorizing Member's default. Therefore, CMESC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with these requirements in SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18)(iv)(C) regarding facilitating access to the clearance and settlement services of all eligible secondary market transactions, including by indirect participants.
B. CMESC's Statement on Burden on Competition
CMESC does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is designed to improve the Rules' accuracy and clarity for Members and Users, to enhance the default management process, and to be consistent with the Act. These proposed changes would not affect CMESC's operations that are already provided in the existing Rules or create additional rights and obligations of Members and Users. As such, CMESC does not believe the proposed rule change would have any impact on burden on competition that does not already exist under the existing Rules or is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. CMESC's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
CMESC currently does not have any Members or Users and has not received nor solicited any written comments from others related to this proposal. CMESC has not received any unsolicited written comments from any interested parties. If any written comments are received, they will be publicly filed as an Exhibit 2 to this filing, as required by Form 19b-4 and the General Instructions thereto.
Persons submitting comments are cautioned that, according to Section IV (Solicitation of Comments) of the Exhibit 1A in the General Instructions to Form 19b-4, the Commission does not edit personal identifying information from comment submissions. Commenters should submit only information that they wish to make available publicly, including their name, email address, and any other identifying information.
All prospective commenters should follow the Commission's instructions on how to submit comments, available at
https://www.sec.gov/​regulatory-actions/​how-to-submit-comments
.
General questions regarding the rule filing process or logistical questions regarding this filing should be directed to the Main Office of the Commission's Division of Trading and Markets at
tradingandmarkets@sec.gov
or 202-551-5777. CMESC reserves the right to not respond to any comments received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Within 45 days of the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
or within such longer period up to 90 days (i) as the Commission may designate if it finds such longer period to be appropriate and publishes its reasons for so finding or (ii) as to which the self-regulatory organization consents, the Commission will:
(A) by order approve or disapprove such proposed rule change, or
(B) institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views, and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act.
(
printed page 66590)
Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments

.
Please include File Number SR-CMESC-2026-011 on the subject line.

All submissions should refer to File Number SR-CMESC-2026-011. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106683; File No. SR-CboeEDGX-2026-071]
October 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 13, 2026, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
3
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
4
]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe EDGX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend Rule 11.1(a)(3) to describe when unpriced orders are eligible for execution and to amend Rule 11.6(q)(2) to clarify the expiration of Day Orders entered during the Overnight Trading Session or Order Acceptance Queueing Time. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's
(
printed page 66597)
website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​edgx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.1(a)(3) to introduce rule text to describe when orders that do not contain a limit price are eligible for execution. Under current Rule 11.1(a)(1), the Exchange does not accept Market Orders,
[
5
]
other than those with a Time-in-Force (“TIF”) instruction of Regular Hours Only
[
6
]
or a Stop Price, prior to 4:00 a.m. Eastern Time or prior to 7:00 a.m. Eastern Time for orders eligible for a 7:00 a.m. Start.
[
7
]
As part of the Exchange's transition to trading 23 hours per day, 5 days per week (“23x5 Trading”), the Exchange updated Rule 11.1(a) to introduce a new subparagraph (3) titled “Orders Permitted in Each Session.”
[
8
]
Rule 11.1(a)(3), which is approved but not yet effective, states: “Market Orders, other than those designated with a Time-in-Force instruction of Regular Hours Only or those that include a Stop Price, will not be accepted by the Exchange prior to Regular Trading Hours.” The intent of this sentence was to prevent Market Orders from executing during the Overnight Trading Session
[
9
]
and the Pre-Opening Session,
[
10
]
but the text did not expressly prohibit the Exchange from accepting Market Orders during Regular Trading Hours and executing during the Post-Closing Session,
[
11
]
which experiences similar characteristics regarding liquidity and volume as the current Early Trading Session.
[
12
]
Now, the Exchange proposes to add an additional sentence to the end of Rule 11.1(a)(3) which states: “Orders without a limit price will not be eligible for execution outside of Regular Trading Hours.” The addition of this sentence eliminates any potential ambiguity about when an order that does not contain a limit price will be eligible for execution on the Exchange. In addition, this proposed change is substantially similar to limits on unpriced orders currently in place on Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq”) and NYSE Arca, Inc. (“NYSE Arca”) and differs only in that the Exchange's proposed rule refers to orders without a limit price rather than specifically designating market orders or pegged orders as other market centers have done in their rule text.
[
13
]
The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 11.6(q)(2) to clarify that a Day Order entered during the Order Acceptance Queueing Time
[
14
]
or Overnight Trading Session will expire at the end of Regular Trading Hours on the same business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs, as provided in Rule 11.1(b).
[
15
]
This amendment replaces the phrase “following trading day,” which could be read ambiguously for orders entered after midnight during the Overnight Trading Session, with language that expressly ties the order's expiration to the business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs.
The change is consistent with the Exchange's intent as described in the Original Filing, which introduced the 23x5 Trading framework and explained that “a trading day is deemed to begin at 9:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the preceding calendar day.” Under Rule 11.1(b), a business day includes the Overnight Trading Session on the preceding calendar day, meaning the entire Overnight Trading Session (from 9:00 p.m. through 4:00 a.m.) belongs to the following business day. The proposed amendment merely conforms the Day Order TIF definition to this structural principle and does not alter any operational aspect of Day Order handling.
Specifically, current Rule 11.6(q)(2) provides that a Day Order entered during the Order Acceptance Queueing Time or the Overnight Trading Session “will expire at the end of Regular Trading Hours on the following trading day.” The Exchange proposes to replace “following trading day” with “same business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs, as provided in Rule 11.1(b).” This revision eliminates any potential ambiguity regarding whether an order entered after midnight
i.e.,
during the portion of the Overnight Trading Session occurring on a new calendar day) could be interpreted as expiring on a different business day than intended.
This proposed rule change will become operative in conjunction with the Original Filing. Rules 11.1(a)(3) and 11.6(q)(2) will be amended with the approved rule text in the Original Filing, whereby the Exchange seeks to offer a new Overnight Trading Session. The amended rule text will take effect in December 2026 pending industry readiness. Prior to codifying the amended rule text, the Exchange will file a proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder to amend its rules confirming that the Exchange is able to comply with its obligations under the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder
(
printed page 66598)
during the Overnight Trading Session and that the Equity Data Plans
[
16
]
are prepared to collect, consolidate, process and disseminate quotation and transaction information at all times during the Overnight Trading Session.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act
[
17
]
and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act. Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
18
]
which requires that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes the proposed amendment to Rule 11.1(a)(3) promotes just and equitable principles of trade by establishing uniform standards for order eligibility with respect to orders without a limit price across all trading sessions. The amendment ensures that all Users are subject to the same restrictions regarding the execution of unpriced orders. By codifying that orders without a limit price will not be eligible for execution outside of Regular Trading Hours in the Exchange's rules, Users will have confidence in how their orders will be handled, which promotes fairness and consistency in the execution process.
Further, the Exchange believes this change removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market and protects investors and the public interest by clarifying that orders without a limit price will not be eligible for execution outside of Regular Trading Hours. During extended trading sessions, such as the Overnight Trading Session and the Post-Closing Session, market liquidity and trading volume are typically lower than during Regular Trading Hours. Under these conditions, unpriced orders may experience execution quality issues, such as executions at prices that vary significantly from the prevailing market price or from investor expectations. By limiting the execution of unpriced orders to Regular Trading Hours—when liquidity is greater and price discovery is more robust—the amendment helps ensure that investors receive executions that are more consistent with their expectations and enhances the overall integrity of the market.
Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed amendment to Rule 11.6(q)(2) removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market by eliminating potential ambiguity in the Exchange's rules regarding when Day Orders expire in the 23x5 trading environment. The amendment promotes just and equitable principles of trade and protects investors and the public interest by ensuring that the rule text clearly communicates the Exchange's order handling procedures, reducing the risk of confusion among market participants regarding order lifecycle in the Overnight Trading Session.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intramarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed amendment to Rule 11.1(a)(3) is not being made for competitive reasons, but rather to prohibit the execution of orders that do not contain a limit price in trading sessions where liquidity is limited, which was partially accomplished by existing rule text that prohibits the Exchange from accepting Market Orders prior to Regular Trading Hours. Additionally, the restriction on the execution of unpriced orders outside of Regular Trading Hours applies equally to all Users in that all Users will be subject to the proposed rule.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intermarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed amendment to Rule 11.1(a)(3) is consistent with the approach taken by other national securities exchanges that prohibits the execution of unpriced orders during extended trading sessions. Accordingly, the proposed rule change does not create any competitive imbalance between the Exchange and other trading venues.
Further, the proposed amendment to Rule 11.6(q)(2) is a non-substantive clarification that does not alter any operational aspect of order handling on the Exchange. The proposed rule change neither introduces new requirements for market participants nor modifies the competitive dynamics between the Exchange and other trading venues.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
19
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
20
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
(
printed page 66599)
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
. Please include file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-071 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-071. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-071 and should be submitted on or before November 12, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
21
]
J. Matthew DeLesDernier,
Deputy Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106680; File No. SR-CBOE-2026-080]
October 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 8, 2026, Cboe Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “Cboe Options”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “Cboe Options”) proposes to amend its Fees Schedule to (i) replace the fixed, premium-based transaction fees applicable to Customer, Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer (including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and removing liquidity in Mini-S&P 500 Index (“XSPBX”) binary options with a tier-based constant transaction fee methodology applicable to Index Binaries, as defined in new footnote 55, while retaining the existing per-contract transaction fees for Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM liquidity-adding and manual orders, and (ii) add Investors Exchange LLC (“IEX”) to fee code RD. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
(
printed page 66592)
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​options/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​cone/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend its Fees Schedule, effective October 1, 2026,
[
3
]
to (1) amend the Binary Options
[
4
]
rate table to replace the fixed, premium-based transaction fees currently applicable to XSPBX options with a tier-based constant transaction fee methodology applicable to Index Binaries
[
5
]
for Customer, Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary,
[
6
]
Broker-Dealer
[
7
]
(including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM
[
8
]
orders executed electronically and removing liquidity, while retaining the existing per-contract transaction fees for Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM liquidity-adding and manual orders, together with new footnote 55; and (2) add IEX to fee code RD
[
9
]
within the Routing Fees section of the Fees Schedule.
Index Binaries Transaction Fees
The Fees Schedule currently includes a Rate Table—Binary Options, which sets forth transaction fees for XSPBX options. The current table assesses fixed per-contract transaction fees that vary by capacity and across seven premium ranges (less than $0.04; $0.04-$0.09; $0.10-$0.24; $0.25-$0.75; $0.76-$0.90; $0.91-$0.96; and greater than $0.96). Specifically, Customer orders are assessed $0.04 (fee code D1),
[
10
]
$0.08 (fee code D2),
[
11
]
$0.20 (fee code D3),
[
12
]
and $0.30 (fee code D4)
[
13
]
per contract, with the fee increasing as the premium approaches $0.50 and decreasing symmetrically as the premium approaches $0.00 or $1.00. Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary and Broker-Dealer orders (including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional orders) are assessed $0.10 (fee code N1),
[
14
]
$0.15 (fee code N2),
[
15
]
$0.25 (fee code N3),
[
16
]
and $0.35 (fee code N4)
[
17
]
per contract across the same premium ranges. Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders are assessed $0.10 (fee code H1),
[
18
]
$0.15 (fee code H2),
[
19
]
$0.25 (fee
(
printed page 66593)
code H3),
[
20
]
and $0.35 (fee code H4)
[
21
]
per contract across the same premium ranges when executed electronically and taking liquidity, $0.05 per contract (fee code HA)
[
22
]
when executed electronically and adding liquidity, and $0.15 per contract (fee code HM)
[
23
]
when executed manually.
The Exchange proposes to amend the Rate Table—Binary Options to replace the fixed, premium-based transaction fees currently applicable to XSPBX options with a tier-based constant transaction fee methodology applicable to “Index Binaries,” under which transaction fees for Customer, Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer (including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and removing liquidity, will be calculated using the following formula:
Transaction Fee = ((k*p*(1-p)*c)*m)
where k is the tier-based constant for the applicable capacity; p is the contract price ($0.01-$1.00); c is the number of contracts traded; and m is the contract multiplier (
i.e.,
100). The proposed tier-based constants (k) are as follows:
Customer (capacity code C): 1.2% (fee code HC);
Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer, Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional (capacity codes F, L, B, N, U, and J): 1.4% (fee code HD); and
Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM (capacity code M), Electronic, Removing Liquidity: 1.4% (fee code HB).
Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and adding liquidity and executed manually will continue to be assessed flat per-contract transaction fees of $0.05 (fee code HA) and $0.15 (fee code HM), respectively, which are unchanged from the current fees. The Exchange believes it is reasonable to continue to assess these orders flat per-contract fees rather than fees under the proposed price-based methodology because Market-Makers, DPMs, and LMMs, unlike other market participants, are subject to continuous quoting and other obligations under the Exchange's Rules that require them to provide liquidity across the full range of contract prices, including in contracts priced near $0.50, where the proposed methodology would otherwise result in the highest fees. A flat, low per-contract fee for liquidity-adding electronic executions and manual executions provides Market-Makers, DPMs, and LMMs with fee certainty that does not vary with the price at which they are obligated to quote, which the Exchange believes encourages them to continue to provide tighter and deeper markets in Index Binaries, to the benefit of all market participants. Market-Maker/DPM/LMM electronic orders that remove liquidity do not further these obligations in the same manner and will therefore be subject to the proposed methodology (fee code HB), consistent with other non-Customer capacities. Maintaining the current flat fees for liquidity-adding and manual Market-Maker/DPM/LMM executions also avoids any fee increase for these participants as a result of the proposed change. The Exchange also proposes to adopt new footnote 55, which provides that “Index Binaries include XSPBX,” and to append footnote 55 to each “Index Binaries” product designation in the new rate table. XSPBX will therefore continue to be the only binary option subject to the rate table following the proposed change.
Under the proposed methodology, the transaction fee for an Index Binary is a function of p*(1-p), which is greatest when the contract price is $0.50 and declines symmetrically as the contract price approaches $0.00 or $1.00. The proposed methodology therefore preserves the general shape of the current premium-range fee structure, under which the highest fees apply to contracts priced near $0.50 and the lowest fees apply to contracts priced near $0.00 or $1.00, while replacing seven discrete premium ranges with a continuous calculation based on the actual contract price. The proposed constants are calibrated so that the maximum per-contract fee for each capacity is unchanged. For example, a Customer executing one contract at a price of $0.50 would be assessed ((0.012 × 0.50 × 0.50 × 1) × 100) = $0.30, which is identical to the current $0.30 fee applicable to Customer orders priced between $0.25 and $0.75 (fee code D4). Similarly, a Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary order executing one contract at $0.50 would be assessed ((0.014 × 0.50 × 0.50 × 1) × 100) = $0.35, identical to the current $0.35 fee applicable to such orders priced between $0.25 and $0.75 (fee code N4). At other contract prices, the fee under the proposed methodology will generally be lower than the fee currently assessed for the applicable premium range. For example, a Customer order executing one contract at $0.25 would be assessed $0.225 rather than $0.30; at $0.10, $0.108 rather than $0.20; and at $0.02, approximately $0.024 rather than $0.04. A Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary order executing one contract at $0.25 would be assessed approximately $0.26 rather than $0.35; at $0.10, $0.126 rather than $0.25; and at $0.02, approximately $0.027 rather than $0.10. Because the proposed fee is calculated continuously rather than by premium range, the fee for contracts priced at the upper end of a current premium range may be modestly higher than the current fixed fee for that range (
e.g.,
a Customer order executing one contract at $0.24 would be assessed approximately $0.219 rather than $0.20), but will never exceed the current maximum per-contract fee for the applicable capacity.
The following examples illustrate the per-contract transaction fee that would be assessed under the proposed methodology for a single contract (
i.e.,
c = 1 and m = 100) at various contract prices, by capacity:

At each contract price, Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and adding liquidity would continue to be assessed $0.05 per contract (fee code HA), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed manually would continue to be assessed $0.15 per contract (fee code HM). Because the transaction fee is calculated on a per-contract basis, the total fee for an execution of multiple contracts equals the applicable per-contract fee multiplied by the number of contracts traded. For example, a Customer order executing ten contracts at a contract price of $0.25 would be assessed ((0.012 × 0.25 × 0.75 × 10) × 100) = $2.25.
The Exchange believes that the proposed methodology will simplify and add transparency to binary option pricing on the Exchange by applying a single, objective calculation based on the contract price in place of multiple premium ranges, and will more closely align the transaction fee with the price of the contract at the time of execution. Additionally, by applying the new rate table to Index Binaries as a category, as defined in new footnote 55, the Exchange will be able to apply a consistent fee methodology across index binary options. Any future addition of a product to the definition of Index Binaries in footnote 55 would be the subject of a separate rule filing.
Addition of IEX to Fee Code RD
The Exchange assesses fees in connection with orders routed away to various options exchanges. The Fees Schedule currently lists fee codes and their corresponding transaction fees for certain Customer orders routed to other options exchanges. Currently, under the Routing Fees section of the Fees Schedule, fee code RD is appended to Customer orders routed to AMEX, BOX, EDGX, MIAX, MX2, SPHR, or PHLX (excluding orders in SPY options routed to PHLX), as well as ETF and Equity options, and assesses a charge of $0.25 per contract.
The Exchange's current approach to routing fees is to set forth in a simple manner certain sub-categories of fees that approximate the cost of routing to other options exchanges based on the cost of transaction fees assessed by each venue as well as costs to the Exchange for routing (
i.e.,
clearing fees, connectivity and other infrastructure costs, membership fees, etc.) (collectively, “Routing Costs”). The Exchange monitors the fees charged as compared to the costs of its routing services and adjusts its routing fees and/or sub-categories to ensure that the Exchange's fees result in a rough approximation of overall Routing Costs, and are not significantly higher or lower in any area. Other options exchanges assess routing fees in a similar manner.
The Exchange proposes to amend fee code RD to add applicable Customer orders routed to IEX, a national securities exchange that is launching an options market on October 2, 2026. As proposed, the description of fee code RD would read: “Routed to AMEX, BOX, EDGX, IEX, MIAX, MX2, SPHR, PHLX (excluding SPY), ETF, Equity.” The charge assessed per contract for fee code RD remains the same ($0.25) under the proposed rule change. The proposed change results in an assessment of fees that, given the fees of an away options exchange, is in line with the Exchange's current approach to routing fees,
i.e.,
in a manner that approximates the cost of routing Customer orders to other away options exchanges, based on the general cost of transaction fees assessed by the sub-category of away options exchanges for such orders (as well as the Exchange's Routing Costs). The Exchange notes that routing through the Exchange is optional and that market participants will continue to be able to choose where to route applicable Customer orders.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”) and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
24
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
25
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5) requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination. The Exchange also believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
26
]
which requires that Exchange rules provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Trading Permit Holders and other persons using its facilities.
As a general matter, the Exchange operates in a highly competitive market. The Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”)has repeatedly expressed its preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
27
]
Market participants can readily direct order flow to competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive or incentives to be insufficient. Accordingly, competitive forces constrain the Exchange's transaction fees, and market participants can readily trade on competing venues if they deem pricing levels at those other venues to be more favorable.
Index Binaries Transaction Fees.
The Exchange believes the proposed tier-
(
printed page 66595)
based constant fee methodology for Index Binaries is reasonable. The proposed constants are calibrated so that the maximum per-contract fee for each capacity ($0.30 for Customer orders and $0.35 for Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer (including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders, other than Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders adding liquidity or executed manually) is unchanged from the maximum fee under the current premium-range structure. At most contract prices, the proposed methodology will result in fees that are lower than those currently assessed for the applicable premium range, and while fees for contracts priced at the upper end of certain current premium ranges may be modestly higher, they will not exceed the current maximum fee for the applicable capacity. The proposed methodology is also reasonable because it bases the transaction fee on an objective, transparent calculation using the actual contract price, the number of contracts, and the contract multiplier, which more closely aligns the fee with the price of the contract at execution than a fixed fee applicable across a broad premium range. The Exchange believes it is reasonable to continue to assess Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and adding liquidity, and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed manually, the existing flat fees of $0.05 and $0.15 per contract, respectively, which are unchanged. Market-Makers, DPMs, and LMMs are subject to continuous quoting and other obligations under the Exchange's Rules that other market participants are not, and those obligations require them to provide liquidity across the full range of contract prices, including in contracts priced near $0.50, where the proposed methodology would otherwise assess the highest fees. A flat, low per-contract fee gives these participants fee certainty that does not vary with the price at which they are obligated to quote, which the Exchange believes encourages them to continue to provide tighter and deeper markets in Index Binaries, to the benefit of all market participants. Market-Maker/DPM/LMM electronic orders that remove liquidity do not further these obligations in the same manner and are therefore subject to the proposed methodology, consistent with other non-Customer capacities. Retaining the current flat fees also ensures that Market-Makers, DPMs, and LMMs will not experience a fee increase as a result of the proposed change. The Exchange believes it is reasonable to adopt footnote 55 to define Index Binaries, as it makes clear the products to which the new rate table applies and currently includes only XSPBX, the product to which the current rate table applies.
The Exchange believes the proposed methodology is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because the same formula and the same tier-based constant will apply to all market participants within each applicable capacity. The Exchange believes it is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory to apply a lower constant to Customer orders (1.2%) than to Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer (including Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional), and Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders (1.4%), which is consistent with the current structure, under which Customer orders are generally assessed lower fees than other capacities in each premium range,
[
28
]
and with the longstanding practice of the Exchange and other options exchanges of assessing lower fees to Customer orders, which enhance liquidity for the benefit of all market participants. The Exchange believes it is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory to apply the same 1.4% constant to Clearing Trading Permit Holder Proprietary, Broker-Dealer, Joint Back-Office, Non-Trading Permit Holder Market Maker, and Professional orders, and to Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and removing liquidity, because each of these capacities is currently assessed identical fees in each premium range (fee codes N1 through N4 and H1 through H4, respectively), and the proposed change preserves that parity. The Exchange believes it remains equitable and not unfairly discriminatory to assess lower flat fees to Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM orders executed electronically and adding liquidity, as is the case today, in light of the value that Cboe Options Market-Maker/DPM/LMM liquidity provides to the market and the obligations to which Cboe Options Market-Makers/DPMs/LMMs are subject that other market participants are not.
Addition of IEX to Fee Code RD.
The Exchange believes the proposed change to add IEX to fee code RD is reasonable because the charge assessed per contract for fee code RD remains the same, and the change is designed to assess routing fees for Customer orders routed to IEX in a manner consistent with the Exchange's current approach to routing fees—
i.e.,
in the most appropriate sub-category of fees that approximates the cost of routing to a group of away options exchanges based on the cost of transaction fees assessed by each venue as well as the Exchange's Routing Costs. The Exchange believes the proposed change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because all applicable Customer orders routed to IEX will automatically yield fee code RD and uniformly be assessed the corresponding fee. The Exchange notes that routing through the Exchange is voluntary, and market participants may choose to route orders to IEX directly or through other means.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange does not believe the proposed changes will impose any burden on intramarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed tier-based constant fee methodology for Index Binaries will apply the same formula and the same constant to all market participants within each applicable capacity, and maintains the relative relationships among capacities that exist under the current premium-range structure. The proposed addition of IEX to fee code RD will apply automatically and uniformly to all Trading Permit Holders' applicable Customer orders routed to IEX, which will be assessed the same $0.25 per contract charge that applies to orders routed to other exchanges within fee code RD. To the extent Customer orders continue to be assessed lower fees than non-Customer orders, and Market-Maker orders adding liquidity in Index Binaries continue to be assessed lower flat fees, the Exchange believes such differentiation is consistent with longstanding industry practice and reflects the value that Customer order flow and Market-Maker liquidity provide to the market.
The Exchange does not believe the proposed changes will impose any burden on intermarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. As previously discussed, the Exchange operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can
(
printed page 66596)
readily direct order flow to competing venues, including 17 other options exchanges and off-exchange venues, if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive or incentives to be insufficient. With respect to the proposed changes to the Index Binaries transaction fees, the Exchange notes that Index Binaries, which currently include only XSPBX, are proprietary products exclusively listed on the Exchange. Because Index Binaries are not listed or traded on any other exchange, the proposed changes to the Index Binaries transaction fees do not implicate intermarket competition. With respect to the addition of IEX to fee code RD, routing through the Exchange is optional, and the charge assessed under fee code RD is unchanged. The Exchange notes that its market share in the options market is subject to competition, and that, in such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and to attract order flow. Moreover, the Commission has recognized that competition for order flow among exchanges is robust. In
NetCoalition
v.
SEC,
the D.C. Circuit stated that “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce,'” and that, “[a]s the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers' . . . .”
[
29
]
Accordingly, the Exchange does not believe its proposed fee changes impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
30
]
and paragraph (f) of Rule 19b-4
[

]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:

All submissions should refer to file number SR-CBOE-2026-080. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CBOE-2026-080 and should be submitted on or before November 12, 2026.

.

33 CFR 165.1321(c)(1)

Vessels 20 meters or greater in length should seek permission from the Captain of the Port or a Designated Representative at least four hours in advance. Title:
Qualified Contributions to a Scholarship Granting Organizations Under Section 25F.
OMB Control Number:
1545-2335.
Form Number:
15714.
Regulation Project Number:
Treasury Decision 10057, Revenue Procedure 2026-6.
Abstract:
Section 25F of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) allows States to voluntarily elect to participate in the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit (FSTC) program. States must provide the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) with a list of the scholarship granting organizations (SGOs) located in their State that meet the requirements of
IRC section 25F
(c)(5). Form 15714 provides an authorized State representative with a method to elect participation under
IRC section 25F
. Revenue Procedure 2026-6 provides guidance regarding a procedure for a State to voluntarily elect to participate under
IRC section 25F
. T.D. 10057 provides rules for State elections to participate under section 25F, including the registration process on the IRS State section 25F portal; rules for information and certifications a State is required to provide for each organization included on the State SGO list; and procedures a State must use in determining whether organizations meet the requirements of section 25F(c)(5). In addition, T.D. 10057 provides procedures for registering SGOs through an IRS electronic SGO portal; reporting, recordkeeping, and third-party disclosure of qualified contributions received by SGOs; and providing timely written acknowledgments to donors.
